questions.title: String Case Transformation
questions.question: Demonstrate character casing transformation by converting a mixed-case string into uppercase with `toUpperCase()` and lowercase with `toLowerCase()`, displaying both results.
questions.explanation: Java's `String.toUpperCase()` and `String.toLowerCase()` methods create and return newly allocated `String` objects containing case-adjusted characters, leaving the original string unchanged due to immutability[cite: 18, 20]. Internally, these methods use character mapping tables defined by the Unicode standard[cite: 4, 20]. When no `Locale` argument is passed, Java uses the host environment's default locale[cite: 8]. In production environments—especially when formatting language-neutral identifiers or protocol headers—specifying `Locale.ROOT` prevents unintended locale-dependent transformations (such as the Turkish dotted/dotless 'i' rule).

questions.title: Multi-Strategy Substring Extraction
questions.question: Extract and display substrings from a sample string in three distinct ways: starting from a specific index, between two bounding indices, and extracting the trailing $N$ characters.
questions.explanation: The `String.substring()` method provides slice operations across character sequences[cite: 20]. Java provides two overloaded variants: `substring(int beginIndex)` extracts from `beginIndex` through the end of the string, while `substring(int beginIndex, int endIndex)` extracts characters in the half-open interval `[beginIndex, endIndex)` (inclusive of `beginIndex`, exclusive of `endIndex`)[cite: 20]. To extract the last $N$ characters safely, developers compute `str.substring(str.length() - n)`[cite: 8, 20]. If any index is negative, exceeds `length()`, or if `beginIndex > endIndex`, the runtime throws an `IndexOutOfBoundsException`[cite: 18]. Prior to Java 7u6, `substring` shared the parent backing array; modern JVMs allocate a fresh, compacted byte array for the slice[cite: 18].

Use two-argument `str.substring(start, end)` where the character at index `end` is excluded[cite: 20].

questions.explanation: Searching for characters and substrings within text is provided by `indexOf()` and `lastIndexOf()`[cite: 20]. The `indexOf` family scans forward from the beginning of the string (or a specified starting offset) and returns the zero-based index of the first occurrence[cite: 1, 20]. Conversely, `lastIndexOf` scans backward from the end of the string (or a specified offset) and returns the index of the final occurrence[cite: 20]. If the target character or substring is not present, both methods return `-1`[cite: 9, 20]. Both methods accept single character code points as well as `String` sequences[cite: 20].

questions.title: Whitespace Sanitation: trim, strip, and isBlank
questions.question: Demonstrate the differences between legacy `trim()`, modern `strip()`, and `isBlank()` on strings containing leading, trailing, and Unicode whitespace characters.
questions.explanation: Prior to Java 11, developers relied on `String.trim()` to remove leading and trailing whitespace[cite: 20]. However, `trim()` uses an ASCII-bound definition: it strips any character whose codepoint is less than or equal to `\u0020` (ASCII space), failing to remove non-breaking Unicode whitespace like `\u2005` or `\u3000`[cite: 20]. Java 11 introduced `String.strip()`, which checks whitespace using `Character.isWhitespace(codepoint)` to strip both ASCII and Unicode spaces[cite: 20]. Java 11 also added `String.isBlank()`, which returns `true` if a string is empty or contains only whitespace codepoints[cite: 20], replacing the older check `str.trim().isEmpty()`[cite: 20].

When invoked with `CharSequence` arguments (`replace(CharSequence target, CharSequence replacement)`), it searches for literal text matches and substitutes them throughout the string[cite: 20]. Unlike `replaceAll()`, `replace()` treats regex symbols (like `.` or `*`) as literal characters, avoiding regex compilation overhead and syntax errors[cite: 20].

questions.question: Implement the Boyer-Moore-Horspool substring pattern search algorithm using a bad-character shift table, returning the first occurrence offset in $O(N)$ average time.
questions.explanation: The Boyer-Moore-Horspool algorithm optimizes substring search by comparing characters from right to left within the pattern window[cite: 18, 20]. A bad-character shift table `int[] shift = new int[256]` is precomputed: every character is assigned a skip distance of `pattern.length()`, except characters present in the pattern (excluding the final character), which are set to `pattern.length() - 1 - i`[cite: 8, 18, 20]. When a mismatch occurs, the shift table shifts the pattern past non-matching text characters, allowing the algorithm to skip multiple characters in a single step and search large texts in sub-linear average time[cite: 20].
hints: Precompute bad-character shift table: `Arrays.fill(shift, m);` for pattern length `m`[cite: 18].
Populate pattern shifts: `shift[pattern.charAt(i)] = m - 1 - i;` for `i < m - 1`[cite: 18, 20].
Compare characters backward from `m - 1` down to 0, shifting by `shift[text.charAt(align + m - 1)]` on mismatch[cite: 8, 14, 18].
questions.expectedOutput: Pattern offset: 10

questions.title: Levenshtein Distance Calculator
questions.question: Compute the edit distance (minimum insertions, deletions, and substitutions to convert string A to B) using dynamic programming.
questions.explanation: The Levenshtein distance measures edit distance between two character sequences: the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or substitutions required to transform string $A$ into string $B$[cite: 20]. A 2D dynamic programming table `dp[m+1][n+1]` models prefix sub-problems[cite: 9, 20]. Base cases initialize boundaries: `dp[i][0] = i` (deleting all characters) and `dp[0][j] = j` (inserting all characters)[cite: 20]. For inner cells, if `s1.charAt(i - 1) == s2.charAt(j - 1)`, cost is 0 (`dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`)[cite: 18, 20]. Otherwise, it takes $1 + \min$ of deletion (`dp[i-1][j]`), insertion (`dp[i][j-1]`), and substitution (`dp[i-1][j-1]`), completing in $O(M \times N)$ time[cite: 3, 20].
hints: Initialize `dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1]` with boundary indices[cite: 9, 20].
If characters match, carry over diagonal: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`[cite: 18, 20].
On mismatch, take `1 + Math.min(deletion, Math.min(insertion, substitution))`[cite: 3, 20].

questions.title: Template Interpolation Engine
questions.question: Implement a template engine that replaces variable placeholders formatted as `${variableName}` with values from a lookup map using index-based string slicing.
questions.explanation: Template interpolation parses and substitutes dynamic placeholders like `${var}` within template text[cite: 20]. Using a `while` loop with `indexOf("${", cursor)` and `indexOf("}", startIdx)`, the engine finds placeholder boundaries[cite: 15, 20]. Literal text before the placeholder is appended to a `StringBuilder`[cite: 3, 20]. The variable name between `${` and `}` is extracted with `substring()`, retrieved from the lookup map, and appended to the output[cite: 3, 20]. The cursor then advances past the closing `}`[cite: 20]. This index-based approach runs in $O(N)$ time without regular expression compilation overhead[cite: 18, 20].

Locate closing brace using `template.indexOf("}", start)`[cite: 20].
Extract key name with `template.substring(start + 2, end)` and look up in map[cite: 3, 20].

questions.title: Quoted CSV Field Parsing Engine
questions.question: Implement a CSV parser that splits fields by commas while preserving commas contained inside quoted strings (e.g., `123, "Doe, John", 45`) using character traversal.
questions.explanation: Standard `String.split(",")` fails on CSV lines containing quoted fields like `101, "Smith, Jane", 45`, because it splits inside the quoted name[cite: 8, 20]. A robust parser uses a state machine to track quote state character by character[cite: 8, 20]. An `inQuotes` boolean flag toggles whenever a double-quote character `"` is encountered[cite: 8]. When a comma `,` is scanned while `inQuotes` is `false`, it marks a field boundary, and the current token buffer is flushed to the result list[cite: 3, 8]. Comma characters encountered while `inQuotes` is `true` are treated as literal characters and appended to the active field[cite: 8], parsing quoted CSV records accurately in linear time[cite: 18, 20].
hints: Track quote boundaries with an `inQuotes = !inQuotes` boolean toggle on `"`[cite: 8].
Only treat commas as field separators when `!inQuotes`[cite: 8].
Trim surrounding quotes from fields before adding them to the result list[cite: 8, 20].

questions.title: Longest Common Subsequence
questions.question: Find the length and reconstructed string of the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) between two strings using dynamic programming and character retrieval.
questions.explanation: The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) finds the longest sequence of characters that appear in the same relative order in two strings, without requiring them to be contiguous[cite: 20]. A 2D dynamic programming table `dp[m+1][n+1]` stores optimal prefix lengths[cite: 9, 20]. If `s1.charAt(i-1) == s2.charAt(j-1)`, the length increases: `dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]`[cite: 18, 20]. If they differ, it takes the maximum of skipping a character from either string: `Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`[cite: 3, 20]. Once the table is populated, backtracking from `dp[m][n]` to `dp[0][0]` reconstructs the actual subsequence string[cite: 20], completing in $O(M \times N)$ time[cite: 20].
hints: Populate `dp[m+1][n+1]` using `dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]` when characters match[cite: 18, 20].
Take `Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])` when characters differ[cite: 3, 20].
Backtrack through the DP table from `(m, n)` to reconstruct the common subsequence string[cite: 20].
